description: 5 HARD-level code questions on Basic Python Syntax (Part 2 of 2). print() separators/end, unexpected indent, the pass statement, and triple-quoted string semantics. Computed outputs verified with Python 3.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

print("a", "b")
print("c")
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
a b
c

EXPLANATION:
print() separates multiple arguments with a space by default (sep=" ") and appends a newline by default (end="\n"). The first call prints "a b" plus a newline; the second call prints "c" plus a newline, so the output is two lines.

code:
print("a", "b")   # sep=" " -> "a b", end="\n"
print("c")          # "c\n"

# Output:
# a b
# c

WHY IT MATTERS:
In Python 2, print "a", "b" behaved differently than print("a", "b") (which printed a tuple). Understanding the defaults of sep and end helps you predict output exactly and control formatting without string concatenation.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

print("x", "y", sep="-", end="!")
print("z")
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
x-y!z

EXPLANATION:
Inside the first call, sep="-" joins x and y with a dash -> "x-y". end="!" replaces the usual newline, so the cursor stays on the same line after the "!". The second print("z") then writes z and its own newline, giving one line: x-y!z.

code:
print("x", "y", sep="-", end="!")  # "x-y" then "!" instead of \n
print("z")                            # "z\n" continues on the same line

# Output:
# x-y!z

WHY IT MATTERS:
sep and end are how you build CSV-like lines, progress bars, and pretty logs without building strings manually:
print(*row, sep=",")          # CSV row
print("\rLoading...", end="") # stay on the same line
If end is changed, the next print continues on the SAME line - many output-formatting bugs come from forgetting which print owns the newline.

questions.question:
What happens when this code runs?

x = 5
  print(x)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
IndentationError: unexpected indent

EXPLANATION:
Line 2 has leading spaces, but it is not the start of an indented block - there is no header line ending with a colon (like if, for, def) above it. Python detects the stray indentation and raises IndentationError at parse time, so the program never runs.

code:
x = 5
  print(x)   # IndentationError: unexpected indent

WHY IT MATTERS:
The error is raised at COMPILE time, before any line executes. Mixing tabs and spaces can also raise TabError: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation. The fix is always: 4 spaces everywhere, never tabs. Paste code between editors that convert tabs to spaces to avoid this class of bug.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

if 10 > 5:
    pass
print("done")
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
done

EXPLANATION:
pass is a no-op statement - it does absolutely nothing but legally occupies the block, because an empty indented block is a SyntaxError. The condition 10 > 5 is True, so the block is entered, pass executes (no effect), then "done" prints.

code:
if 10 > 5:
    pass        # valid placeholder - empty blocks are NOT allowed
print("done")   # done

WHY IT MATTERS:
pass is used as a placeholder during development (stub bodies), in exception handlers you intend to ignore, and in abstract method stubs. It is different from continue (skips to the next loop iteration) and from a plain comment (a comment would NOT make a bare block valid).

questions.question:
This code looks like it has a comment. What does it print?

"""This is documentation."""
print("hello")
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
hello

EXPLANATION:
The triple-quoted string is NOT a comment - it is a string expression statement. Python evaluates the string and immediately discards the value, so it has no visible effect, and "hello" prints normally. A real comment starts with # and produces no object.

code:
"""This is documentation."""  # a string object is created, then thrown away
print("hello")                  # hello

WHY IT MATTERS:
The same syntax becomes a docstring only when it is the FIRST statement of a module, class, or function - tooling then reads it via obj.__doc__. Somewhere else it is dead code. Putting a triple-quoted "comment" inside a loop is a real (if minor) performance anti-pattern because Python still allocates the string each iteration.
